## Appendix H Current Limitations

Currently, CHAL operates exclusively in an adversarial debate mode. While effective for stress-testing beliefs, this does not exhaust the space of useful dialectical interactions. For example, a collaborative truth-seeking mode, in which agents cooperate to resolve disagreements and align on an agreed-upon solution, or a moderated mode, in which a guiding agent steers agents through the most relevant sub-topics of a query, could potentially yield deeper analysis. CHAL’s modular architecture is designed to accommodate such extensions as toggleable modes and is a direction for future work.

Computational cost is a practical constraint. As noted in Section 4.1, the number of adjudicated pairs scales on the order of \mathcal{O}\left(RSN^{2}\right) , quadratically in the council size N and linearly in rounds R and challenges per pair S . A single five-round, two-agent debate using OpenAI’s o4-mini cost us approximately $2, so scaling to larger council sizes for more rounds incurs meaningful cost with the strongest frontier reasoning models.

At the implementation level, the structured CBS outputs also impose strict formatting requirements enforced through a multi-phase validation process. As such, failed outputs trigger retries with corrective feedback, increasing latency and token consumption. Frontier models handle these constraints reliably, but smaller or open-source models may struggle to produce well-formed CBS objects consistently, limiting the range of models that can currently serve as council members without further prompt engineering or fine-tuning. This is another direction for future software refinement of CHAL.

Finally, CHAL’s current meta-cognitive library (thirteen epistemic personas, eight logic systems, and six ethics frameworks) is an initial set sufficient to demonstrate systematic effects of meta-cognitive parameterization. However, there are many agent personas and systems that could be integrated as viable options for CHAL to choose from, as well as further refining the prompting architecture of the pipeline as a whole. CHAL is designed as a general research platform to which the community can contribute additional configurations, and expanding this library is a natural direction for future development and research.

An agent’s epistemic position determines its standards for evidence, justification, and inference, including what kinds of reasons it takes to be compelling, how it weighs competing sources of knowledge, and where it locates the burden of proof. In CHAL, epistemic personas are assigned exclusively to the LLM council agents rather than the adjudicator (see Section 4 for formalism), whose evaluation is governed instead by independently configured logic and ethics systems. This separation is deliberate: the council’s role is to generate and defend positions from genuinely distinct epistemological starting points, while the adjudicator’s role is to evaluate the argumentative exchange against a fixed and consistent standard. By populating the council with agents reasoning from competing epistemological traditions, CHAL explores the belief space more broadly than any single framework would permit, as illustrated in Figures 1(a) and 1(b).

CHAL currently provides twelve epistemic personas, eight logic systems, and six ethical systems, each grounded in established philosophical traditions. The default logic system, Classical + Informal + Bayesian (CIB), combines deductive validity with inductive and abductive support weighted by prior probability. Logic and ethics scores are computed independently by an adjudicator agent and combined via user-specified weights (see Section 4.2). The choice of system materially affects adjudication outcomes and is therefore a primary variable of interest for empirical studies of debate dynamics. Summary tables and complete descriptions for all epistemic positions as well as logical and ethical systems are provided in Appendix B.
